outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction to LLMs in Tabular Learning
outline.description: The landscape of artificial intelligence has historically been divided between two dominant paradigms: the manipulation of sequential textual data and the analysis of structured tabular data. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized the former, the latter remains a critical frontier for real-world decision-making systems. Understanding the distinction between these data modalities is essential before attempting to bridge them. Tabular data, ubiquitous in fields ranging from healthcare diagnostics and financial risk assessment to manufacturing quality control, consists of rows representing distinct observations and columns representing specific attributes or features. outline.description: In the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence, the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into tabular data analysis represents a paradigm shift away from purely statistical pattern matching toward reasoning-driven feature synthesis. Conventional approaches to tabular learning often rely on heavy computational architectures or extensive fine-tuning to achieve competitive performance, particularly in low-data regimes. However, the unique capacity of LLMs to synthesize vast amounts of textual prior knowledge creates an opportunity to rethink the fundamental pipeline of machine learning. outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Prompt Engineering for Structured Reasoning
outline.description: In the realm of automated feature engineering using Large Language Models (LLMs), the efficacy of the system hinges critically on the precision and structure of the input prompts. Unlike standard conversational interactions where flexibility is paramount, the \textsf{FeatLLM} framework demands a highly disciplined approach to prompt construction to transform raw tabular data into meaningful, executable logic. The core philosophy behind this methodology is to treat the LLM not merely as a text generator, but as a simulated domain expert capable of decomposing complex classification problems into discrete, interpretable rules.
